title: The Reformation and Counter-Reformation
orientation: This short chapter treats the Reformation and Counter-Reformation together as twin revolts of 'less civilized' northern and Spanish Europe against the intellectual and moral authority of Renaissance Italy. Russell argues that, philosophically, the century the Reformation opens is a barren one -- its great figures, Luther, Calvin, and Loyola, are medieval in outlook -- but that its political and theological consequences (the growth of state power over religion, and eventually religious exhaustion leading to toleration) matter more for the history of philosophy than any doctrine the reformers themselves produced.
historical_background: Russell frames the Reformation as German and the Counter-Reformation as Spanish, with the wars of religion doubling as wars between Spain and its enemies during the height of Spanish power. Northern moral indignation against the 'easy-going laxity' of the Borgias and Medici popes fed both movements; an English saying of the period held that 'An Englishman Italianate / Is a devil incarnate,' and Russell notes how often Shakespeare's villains (Iago, Iachimo) are Italians. The Reformation rejected the Pope's authority outright; the Counter-Reformation left papal power intact -- indeed enhanced it -- while purging the Renaissance-era laxity the Curia had tolerated.
philosophical_problems: What is the proper relationship between the individual soul and God, independent of the institutional Church?
Should ultimate authority over religion in a nation rest with the Pope, with the state/monarch, or with the individual conscience?
Is salvation determined by predestination (independent of works) or by a combination of free will and works?
How does prolonged religious warfare, rather than theological argument, produce religious toleration?

philosophers_discussed.name: Martin Luther
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented as reverting to Saint Augustine's theology of the soul's relation to God (but not Augustine's view of the Church), abolishing purgatory and indulgences, teaching predestination, and -- despite intending only to weaken the Church -- accelerating the growth of princely power by recognizing Protestant rulers as heads of their national Churches. Russell quotes his outraged reaction to Copernicus in the following chapter, but here treats him chiefly as a theological and political figure.

philosophers_discussed.name: John Calvin
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Grouped with Luther as reverting to an Augustinian emphasis on the soul's direct relation to God and on predestination, while rejecting purgatory, indulgences, and papal authority; his followers are cited (in the chapter's political discussion) as an example of the individualist wing of Protestantism resistant to any external authority, whether Pope or king.

philosophers_discussed.name: Ignatius of Loyola
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Founder of the Jesuit order, credited by Russell with checking the 'amazingly rapid' early success of Protestantism through the Jesuits' military-style discipline, missionary zeal, skill as confessors, and especially their dominance of education (the same Jesuit education, Russell notes, that would later teach Descartes more mathematics than he could have learned elsewhere). Doctrinally, Loyola and the Jesuits opposed predestination, affirmed free will, and held that salvation requires both faith and works.

schools_discussed: The Society of Jesus (Jesuits) and Counter-Reformation Catholicism

core_concepts.name: Predestination versus free will and works
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Protestants, following the part of Saint Augustine's theology that concerns the soul's fate, taught that whether a soul is saved or damned is fixed by God in advance (predestination), regardless of a priest's or the individual's own actions. The Jesuits taught the opposite: humans have genuine free will, and salvation comes from both faith and good works, not faith alone.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Predestination: the doctrine that God has eternally and unconditionally determined the salvation or damnation of each soul, independent of the actions of priests or, in the strict Calvinist form, of the individual's own deeds. The Jesuit counter-doctrine held that free will is real and that salvation requires both faith and works, directly rejecting the Augustinian strand the Reformers emphasized.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It reshaped the practical power of the clergy: if salvation does not depend on priestly intervention (masses, indulgences), the Church's economic and spiritual hold over believers weakens, which is why Russell treats predestination as politically as much as theologically significant.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Rooted in Saint Augustine's theology, revived selectively by Luther and Calvin in the sixteenth century and rejected by the Jesuits at and after the Council of Trent.
examples: The abolition of purgatory and the rejection of Indulgences, both of which had depended on the idea that priestly/papal action could affect a soul's fate
objections: The Jesuit position that predestination is false and that free will and works matter
competing_positions: The Jesuit doctrine of free will and salvation by faith and works
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The dispute over free will and predestination recurs later in the book's treatment of Hobbes's determinism and of theological controversies surrounding Descartes and his contemporaries.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious in origin but with immediate political consequences for clerical power, discussed below.

core_concepts.name: The paradoxical weakening of clerical power by Protestant theology
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Even though Luther and Calvin were just as dogmatic as Catholic theologians, their doctrines (abolishing purgatory, rejecting indulgences, teaching predestination) removed the mechanisms by which priests could claim to influence an individual's salvation. This meant Protestant Churches, even in Protestant countries, never became as powerful as the Catholic Church was in Catholic countries.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's claim: 'These innovations, while they helped in the struggle with the Pope, prevented the Protestant Churches from becoming as powerful in Protestant countries as the Catholic Church was in Catholic countries. Protestant divines were... just as bigoted as Catholic theologians, but they had less power, and were therefore less able to do harm.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It explains why, despite equally dogmatic clergy on both sides, Protestant countries developed more intellectual liberty over time -- not because Protestant theologians were more tolerant in spirit, but because their doctrines structurally reduced institutional clerical power.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A direct consequence of the theological choices of the early Reformation.
examples: Abolition of purgatory (removing the rationale for paid masses for the dead)
Rejection of Indulgences (removing a major source of papal revenue)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up the following chapter's account of why the seventeenth-century scientific revolution found more room to flourish, and eventually more tolerance, in Protestant countries such as Holland and England.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central: theology here is shown determining institutional political power, not just personal belief.

core_concepts.name: The state's authority over the national Church (Erastian tendency)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Once the Pope's universal authority was rejected, someone had to take his place as head of the Church within each Protestant nation. Luther was willing to let the local prince fill that role, which is exactly what happened in England, Germany, Scandinavia, and (after independence) Holland, accelerating the general growth of royal and state power.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell describes Luther as 'willing, wherever the prince was Protestant, to recognize him as head of the Church in his own country,' citing Henry VIII and Elizabeth in England and the Protestant princes of Germany, Scandinavia, and Holland as examples; this 'accelerated the already existing tendency to increase in the power of kings.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It links the Reformation directly to early modern state-building and to the later conflicts (such as the English Civil War) over whether the state or individual conscience should have final authority in religion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Emerges directly from Luther's rejection of papal authority combined with his willingness to substitute princely authority for it.
examples: Henry VIII and Elizabeth I asserting headship of the Church of England
Protestant princes of Germany, Scandinavia, and Holland doing likewise
objections: Individualist Protestants (including the Anabaptists, and later the English Puritans in conflict with Cromwell and the Long Parliament) who were as unwilling to submit to the king as to the Pope
competing_positions: The individualist wing of the Reformation, which rejected state control of religion just as it rejected papal control
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates the political theory of Hobbes (Book III, Chapter VIII), who argues the sovereign must also control religion, and the English constitutional conflicts of the seventeenth century.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: This concept is explicitly about the fusion of political and religious authority.

core_concepts.name: Religious toleration as the exhausted product of the wars of religion
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell argues that toleration did not arise from theological argument but from sheer war-weariness: decades of religious warfare convinced people that forcing doctrinal unity was not worth the cost, and this weariness fed directly into eighteenth- and nineteenth-century liberalism.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's claim: 'Gradually weariness resulting from the wars of religion led to the growth of belief in religious toleration, which was one of the sources of the movement which developed into eighteenth- and nineteenth-century liberalism.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It offers a non-idealist, historically grounded account of how a major liberal value (toleration) actually originated -- from exhaustion rather than from philosophical conviction -- which is characteristic of Russell's broader method of tying ideas to their political and social causes.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A cumulative effect of decades of religious warfare, most notably (per the chapter's final paragraph) the Thirty Years' War.
examples: The conflict between Cromwell and the Long Parliament, partly a conflict over whether the state should decide religious matters
The eventual realization after the Thirty Years' War that neither Protestants nor Catholics could achieve total victory
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Feeds into the following chapter's account of the seventeenth-century flourishing of science and of the argument, developed later in the book, that toleration was a precondition for Enlightenment liberalism.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central; toleration here is presented as a political and social outcome, not a theological doctrine.

core_concepts.name: The Jesuit method: discipline, education, and missionary zeal
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Loyola, a former soldier, organized the Jesuit order on military lines, with strict obedience to the General and a self-conception of waging 'warfare against heresy.' Their effectiveness came less from theology than from organization: disciplined propaganda, skillful and lenient confession practice, missionary success (especially in the Far East), and above all excellent education, which gave them a lasting hold on the minds of the young.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's summary: the Jesuits 'were disciplined, able, completely devoted to the cause, and skilful propagandists'; 'whenever theology did not interfere, the education they gave was the best obtainable.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is Russell's explanation for how the Counter-Reformation checked Protestantism's early rapid success; it also sets up a direct narrative link forward, since Jesuit education is credited with teaching Descartes more mathematics than he could otherwise have learned.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Founded by Ignatius of Loyola; influential from the Council of Trent onward.
examples: Jesuit missionary work in the Far East
Jesuit dominance of education, later benefiting Descartes
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly foreshadows Chapter IX's account of Descartes's Jesuit education at La Flèche.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The Jesuits also urged Catholic princes toward persecution and helped re-establish the Inquisition, including in Italy.

arguments.title: The Reformation and Counter-Reformation as parallel but different revolts against Italy
premises: Both movements represent 'the rebellion of less civilized nations against the intellectual domination of Italy.'
In the Reformation, the revolt was political and theological: papal authority was rejected outright and papal revenue withheld.

In the Counter-Reformation, the revolt was only against the moral and intellectual freedom of Renaissance Italy; papal power itself was not diminished but enhanced, purged of Borgia-and-Medici-style laxity.
arguments.conclusion: The Reformation (broadly German) and the Counter-Reformation (broadly Spanish) are best understood as two different reactions to the same underlying resentment of Italian cultural and moral authority, one rejecting the Pope, the other reforming around him.
arguments.explanation: Russell supports this with the English saying about Italianate villainy and Shakespeare's Italian villains as evidence of how deeply moral indignation against Italy had penetrated northern culture, feeding directly into the Reformation's energy, even though this indignation also caused an unfortunate 'intellectual repudiation of what Italy had done for civilization.'
implications: Explains why the chapter treats the wars of religion as simultaneously wars between Spain and its enemies.
Helps explain why, philosophically, the century is 'barren': both movements were reactive and backward-looking (medieval), not creative.

arguments.title: Protestant theology unintentionally limited Protestant clerical power
premises: Luther and Calvin abolished purgatory and rejected Indulgences, removing the mechanisms (masses for the dead, sale of pardons) by which priests and the papacy affected souls' fates and drew revenue.
The doctrine of predestination made a soul's fate after death independent of any priest's actions.
These theological choices were adopted mainly as weapons in the struggle against the Pope, not as a deliberate plan to weaken clergy generally.
arguments.conclusion: As an unintended side effect, Protestant Churches never became as powerful in Protestant countries as the Catholic Church was in Catholic countries, even though Protestant divines were, in Russell's view, just as bigoted.
arguments.explanation: Because Protestant clergy lost the specific institutional levers (purgatory, indulgences, sacramental control over predestined salvation) that gave the Catholic Church its temporal power, their bigotry had structurally less capacity to translate into coercive institutional power.
implications: This is Russell's causal explanation for why Protestant countries, over time, developed greater freedom of thought -- not because Protestants were more liberal in temperament, but because their own doctrines undercut clerical power.

key_distinctions: Reformation (German, rejects papal authority outright, political and theological) vs. Counter-Reformation (Spanish, rejects only Renaissance-era moral/intellectual laxity, leaves and even strengthens papal power)
Predestination (Protestant, following Augustine's soul-theology) vs. free will and salvation by faith-and-works (Jesuit)

State-controlled national Churches (Luther's position, adopted in England, Germany, Scandinavia, Holland) vs. individualist Protestant resistance to any external authority (Anabaptists, and the Puritan wing in the English Civil War)
Theological bigotry (present on both Protestant and Catholic sides) vs. institutional power to enforce it (structurally reduced for Protestant clergy)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Luther and Calvin are explicitly said to revert to Saint Augustine's theology of the soul's relation to God, while discarding his ecclesiology; the chapter immediately follows and contrasts with the previous chapter's account of Erasmus and More, the moderate humanists whose reformist, non-schismatic temperament the Reformation's polarization made untenable.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The chapter's account of Jesuit education directly foreshadows Descartes's schooling at the Jesuit college of La Flèche (Chapter IX); its account of the state assuming headship of national Churches anticipates Hobbes's Erastian argument in Leviathan (Chapter VIII) that the sovereign must also control religion; and its account of war-weariness producing toleration is presented as a root of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century liberalism.
political_social_context: The chapter foregrounds the entanglement of theology with state power: the rejection of papal tribute, the rise of Protestant princes as heads of national Churches, the acceleration of royal power generally, the Anabaptist and Puritan resistance to both Pope and king, the conflict between Cromwell and the Long Parliament, and the wars of religion understood simultaneously as wars against Spanish power at its height, culminating in the Thirty Years' War.
religion_science_culture_context: Russell stresses that, philosophically, the century following Luther's revolt was 'a barren one,' with Luther, Calvin, and Loyola all 'medieval in philosophy' compared to the Renaissance Italians or to Erasmus and More; the intellectual payoff of the Reformation era, he argues, was ultimately beneficial only in the longer run, once exhaustion from religious war forced the abandonment of the medieval hope for doctrinal unity and turned able men toward secular learning, mathematics, and science -- the subject of the following chapter.
russell_presentation: Russell treats the Reformation and Counter-Reformation as historically important but philosophically barren: Luther, Calvin, and Loyola are 'medieval in philosophy' compared to the Italians or to Erasmus and More. He is notably even-handed in blaming bigotry on both sides ('Protestant divines were... just as bigoted as Catholic theologians') while offering a structural explanation for why Protestant countries nonetheless ended up with more intellectual liberty: not superior tolerance of temperament, but doctrines (rejection of purgatory and indulgences, predestination) that happened to weaken clerical institutional power. He credits the Jesuits with real organizational and educational excellence despite deploring their support for persecution and the Inquisition. His overall verdict is that the immediate intellectual results of this era were 'wholly bad, but ultimately beneficial,' since exhaustion from the wars of religion forced the abandonment of the medieval dream of doctrinal unity and redirected able minds toward science -- the pivot to Chapter VI.
critical_context: Russell's framing of both movements primarily as 'less civilized nations' rebelling against Italy is a deliberately provocative simplification -- later historians of the Reformation give much greater independent weight to economic factors (such as resentment of papal taxation), print culture, vernacular Bible translation, and local political rivalries than this brief chapter allows room for; Russell himself acknowledges the account is compressed, since the chapter is only a short bridge to the seventeenth-century scientific revolution that is his real interest in this part of the book.
key_takeaways: Russell treats the Reformation (German, anti-papal) and Counter-Reformation (Spanish, pro-papal but anti-laxity) as two different revolts against Renaissance Italy's intellectual and moral authority.
Luther, Calvin, and Loyola are all judged 'medieval in philosophy'; the century the Reformation opens is philosophically barren.

Protestant theology (rejecting purgatory and indulgences, teaching predestination) unintentionally weakened clerical institutional power, even though Protestant divines were just as bigoted as Catholic ones.

Luther's willingness to let Protestant princes head national Churches accelerated the growth of royal/state power, provoking a further split between state-aligned Protestants and individualist Protestants (Anabaptists, and later Puritans) unwilling to submit to either Pope or king.

The Counter-Reformation's success against Protestantism owed chiefly to Loyola's Jesuits: their discipline, propaganda skill, missionary zeal, and especially their excellent education (which would later benefit Descartes).
Religious toleration emerged not from theological argument but from exhaustion after the wars of religion, especially the Thirty Years' War, feeding into later liberalism.
study_notes:
This chapter functions as a hinge: it closes out Russell's account of the Renaissance and Reformation era and clears the ground for the seventeenth-century scientific revolution that dominates the rest of Book III. The single most important interpretive move to hold onto is Russell's structural argument about power: theological doctrine (predestination, rejection of purgatory and indulgences) is shown determining institutional power, independent of the personal tolerance or bigotry of the theologians who held it. This is a good example of Russell's characteristic method throughout the History -- explaining the influence of ideas partly through their unintended political and economic consequences, not just their internal logical content.

A second thread worth tracking closely is the question of who controls religion once papal authority is rejected: the state (Luther's answer, realized in England, Germany, Scandinavia, and Holland) or the individual conscience (the Anabaptist and, later, Puritan answer). This tension reappears explicitly in Book III's treatment of Hobbes, who argues forcefully that the sovereign must also be head of religion precisely because divided religious authority breeds civil war -- a worry this chapter shows was not abstract but grounded in the actual conflict between Cromwell and the Long Parliament.

Finally, notice how Russell resists treating toleration as a philosophical achievement of principled argument; he presents it instead as the exhausted byproduct of decades of inconclusive religious war. This deflationary, causally-minded account of the origins of a core liberal value is worth comparing with more idealist histories of toleration you may encounter elsewhere.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The Protestant doctrine that God has already decided, before you are even born, whether your soul will be saved or damned -- nothing a priest (or, in the strict Calvinist version, even you) does can change it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine, revived by Luther and Calvin from a strand of Augustinian theology, that God has eternally and unconditionally determined each soul's salvation or damnation, independent of priestly mediation (sacraments, masses) and, in its strict form, independent of the individual's own works.
related_concepts: Predestination versus free will and works

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Payments or acts of devotion the medieval Catholic Church said could reduce the punishment owed for sin -- a major source of papal revenue that the Reformers rejected as false.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A remission, granted by the Church, of temporal punishment due for sins already forgiven, historically obtainable in part through payment; rejection of Indulgences by Luther and Calvin removed a large source of papal revenue and was central to the early Reformation controversy.
related_concepts: Predestination versus free will and works
The paradoxical weakening of clerical power by Protestant theology

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: In Catholic doctrine, a state after death where souls are purified before entering heaven -- and which could supposedly be shortened by masses said for the dead. Protestants abolished the idea.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Catholic doctrine of an intermediate post-mortem state of purification from which souls could be delivered more quickly through masses and prayers; its abolition by Luther and Calvin removed both a theological claim and an associated ecclesiastical revenue stream.
related_concepts: The paradoxical weakening of clerical power by Protestant theology

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Catholic religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola, organized like an army, dedicated to fighting heresy through education, missionary work, and disciplined obedience -- the main force behind the Counter-Reformation's success.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola on quasi-military lines of strict obedience to the General, influential from the Council of Trent onward through disciplined propaganda, missionary expansion (notably in the Far East), skillful practice as confessors, and dominance of European education; theologically opposed to predestination, affirming free will and salvation by faith and works.
related_concepts: The Jesuit method: discipline, education, and missionary zeal

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what do the Reformation and Counter-Reformation have in common, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: Both represent revolts of 'less civilized nations' against the intellectual domination of Renaissance Italy. They differ in that the Reformation also rejected papal authority and its revenue outright (a political and theological revolt), while the Counter-Reformation left papal power intact -- indeed enhanced it -- and revolted only against the moral and intellectual laxity of Renaissance Italy.
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's opening thesis, framing the Reformation as broadly German and the Counter-Reformation as broadly Spanish.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, did Protestant Churches never become as powerful in Protestant countries as the Catholic Church was in Catholic countries, even though Protestant divines were just as bigoted?
questions.answer: Because the doctrines Luther and Calvin adopted against the Pope (abolishing purgatory, rejecting indulgences, teaching predestination) removed the mechanisms by which priests could claim to affect a soul's fate, structurally reducing clerical power even though the clergy's dogmatism was undiminished.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's causal, structural explanation, distinguishing bigotry of belief from institutional power to enforce it.

questions.prompt: Which figure founded the Jesuit order on military lines and is credited by Russell with checking the early rapid success of Protestantism?
questions.explanation: Loyola had been a soldier, and modeled the order on strict obedience to a General; the Jesuits became disciplined, effective propagandists, educators, and missionaries.

questions.prompt: How did the question of who should control religion divide Protestants almost from the beginning?
questions.answer: Luther was willing to recognize a Protestant prince as head of the Church in his own country (realized in England, Germany, Scandinavia, and Holland), while other Protestants who took the individualistic aspects of the Reformation seriously -- such as the Anabaptists, and later the Puritan side in the conflict between Cromwell and the Long Parliament -- were as unwilling to submit to the king as to the Pope.
questions.explanation: This division over state versus individual authority in religion recurs later in Hobbes's political theory.

questions.prompt: Compare the Protestant and Jesuit positions on predestination and salvation.
questions.answer: Protestants (following Luther and Calvin) taught predestination: a soul's fate is fixed by God regardless of works or priestly action. The Jesuits held the opposite -- they believed in free will and opposed predestination, teaching that salvation comes from both faith and works, not faith alone.
questions.explanation: This was one of the central doctrinal battle lines of the Counter-Reformation.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, how did religious toleration ultimately arise, and what larger movement did it help produce?
questions.answer: It arose gradually from weariness resulting from the wars of religion, not from theological argument, and became one of the sources of the movement that developed into eighteenth- and nineteenth-century liberalism.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's deflationary, historically grounded account of toleration's origin.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's explanation of why the Reformation's theological choices, though aimed at weakening the Pope, ended up limiting Protestant clerical power generally.
questions.answer: Premise 1: Luther and Calvin abolished purgatory and rejected indulgences, removing priestly and papal mechanisms for affecting souls' fates and revenue. Premise 2: predestination made a soul's fate independent of any priest's actions. Premise 3: these were adopted mainly as weapons against the Pope, not as a general anti-clerical program. Conclusion: as an unintended side effect, Protestant clergy, though just as bigoted as Catholic theologians, had structurally less institutional power to do harm.
questions.explanation: This argument exemplifies Russell's method of tracing unintended political consequences of theological doctrine.
